title: Evidence of competing ground states between fractional Chern insulator and antiferromagnetism in moiré MoTe_2

paper_content.abstract:
Moiré materials—formed by stacking atomically thin crystals with a small twist—create
tunable electronic lattices where strong interactions and band topology can generate unusual
magnetic and topological phases. In twisted bilayer MoTe , ferromagnetism has been closely
2
linked to integer and fractional Chern insulators, while the true zero‑field ground state can
be sensitive to twist angle and vertical electric field. Here we show that devices with
intermediate twist angle (~3°) may host antiferromagnetic ordered ground states at fixed
hole fillings of 1 and 2/3, evidenced by suppressed zero‑field magneto‑optical and Hall
responses and field‑driven transitions into quantized Chern states. By tuning only the
vertical electric field, we reversibly switch the system from antiferromagnetism to
ferromagnetism accompanied by integer or fractional Chern insulating behavior near the
layer‑polarization threshold, and then to a paramagnetic regime at larger fields. These
results reveal competing correlated ground states in a single moiré platform and establish
electric‑field control of magnetism and topology.
paper_content.introduction:
The interplay between strong correlations and topology can lead to the emergence of intriguing
quantum states of matter. Moiré materials based on transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) have
emerged as a promising platform for exploring novel quantum phenomena that arise from band
topology and many-body interactions1–12. Recently, there has been a surge in research focused on
rhombohedral-stacked (R-stacked) tMoTe , in which transport experiments have provided
2
unambiguous evidence of both QAH and FQAH effects on devices with relatively large twist
angles 𝜃 ∼ 3.7°−3.9° 13,14. Based on the obtained Chern numbers, photoluminescence and
compressibility measurements suggest the FQAH is the ground state of 𝑣 = 2/3 (𝜈 = 1 is
h h
defined as one hole per moiré unit cell, corresponding to a half-filled moiré valence band) over a
relatively large range of twist angle, specifically 𝜃~2.6°−3.9°, while QAH at 𝑣 = 1 extends
h
even down to 2.1°14–19. The Chern numbers were obtained by comparing the Streda formula with
the fitted dispersion slope of the filling factor versus the magnetic field (𝐵 ) of Tesla order.
However, the energy difference between the competing phases is usually subtle, and the applied
relatively large 𝐵 could hide the true ground state at zero 𝐵. Transport measurement can provide
unambiguous evidence of the true ground state as demonstrated in devices with relatively large
twist angles (𝜃 ∼ 3.7°−3.9°), while transport study of 𝑣 ≤ 1 states in tMoTe moiré device with
h 2
small 𝜃 is challenging due to the increasing difficulty of making transparent electrical contact. On
the other hand, in the moiré system, the ground states are usually expected to be sensitive to the
twist angle22, suggesting more unexpected correlated effects to explore in tMoTe moiré system
2
with smaller 𝜃19–24.

In this work, we performed a systematic twist angle dependence study on the R-stacked tMoTe
2
moiré system by combining optical and transport measurements. We observed competing magnetic
ground states depending on both twist angle and 𝐸. Specifically, we observed unexpected AFM
ground states with vanishing Hall resistance at both 𝑣 = 1 and 2/3, at intermediate twist angles
h
𝜃~3° , in between the FMCCI ground states of both larger and smaller 𝜃 . Moreover, applying
vertical electric field (𝐸) induces an AFM to FM (ICICFCI) transition and an emergent FM state
was observed near critical electric field (𝐸 ) of layer polarization.

Optical measurements
The optical measurements were performed in reflection geometry in a home-built confocal optical
microscope system based on a closed-cycle helium cryostat (base temperature 1.6 K) equipped
with a superconducting magnet (9 T). A superluminescent light-emitting diode with a peak
wavelength of 1070 nm and full width at half-maximum bandwidth of 90 nm was used as the
light source. The output of the diode was coupled to a single-mode fiber and focused onto the

λ

NA

reflected light of a given helicity was spectrally resolved by a spectrometer coupled to a liquid
nitrogen-cooled InGaAs one-dimensional array sensor (Princeton Instruments PyLoN-IR 1.7).
The reflectance contrast spectrum was obtained by comparing the reflected light spectrum from the
sample with the reference spectrum measured on a heavily doped condition (which is featureless

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The authors present a detailed study of tMoTe2 by tuning the twisting angle and vertical electric field, along with changing temperatures and magnetic fields, probed by both optical and electrical approaches. They focus on the magnetic states for samples of different conditions. The data sets are rich. There are a few major aspects the authors can improve before further consideration of this manuscript.
1. tMoTe2 is a system being intensively studied in the scientific field. What are the missing parts this work can contribute to? From both abstract and introduction, it is unclear what the new things this work brought to the community. The authors started with a brief introduction in abstract and introduction that tMoTe2 is a rich system in support of AQHE, but suddenly switched to talk about magnetism they found in this work. Some missing parts need to be provided so the readers can appreciate this work in the context of what has been and not been achieved in the field.
2. The readability of most figures is still low. It seems that figure 1d-f and 1g-I have one-to-one corresponding relationship. However, from these sub-figures themselves, it is hard to read since g and h have the same legend yet different curves. The same issue is for Figure b and c (these two sub-figures have the same noted curves), d and e. It is good to add brief legends to indicate the different conditions, based on which these data were acquired.
3. Mechanism. The authors suggest “charge transfer” as the mechanism. What are the charge transfer coming from? It is transferred from metal electrode to the tMoTe2, or self doping by transfer between the two layers of tMoTe2? Why is it not because of electric field effect? The authors have top and bottom electrodes, which allow them to separate electric field and electrostatic doping effects by tuning the top and bottom electrodes separately. They should do this experiment and analysis.
4. It is possible that the AFM magnetization orientation is out of plane, as the author speculated. But the author’s argument for this speculation appears problematic. The authors thought if it is in-plane, the MCD should keep constant while B field is applied out of plane, which is not true. If the magnetic anisotropy is in-plane, it is likely the out of plane B field would gradually increase the MCD, and it is also likely that out of plane B field would cause spin flop effect suddenly at a certain B field.
5. Multiple typos need to be fixed. “inplane” is not a word, should be in plane or in-plane. “our-of-plane” should be out-of-plane. “Honeycomb” (main text) and “Magnetic” (figure 1 caption) should not be capitalized in sentences.
6. Finally, the authors for a few times stressed the “unexpected” AFM states. Why is it unexpected? I felt the field of study has reported such magnetic states many times in different twisting systems. If I am wrong, please correct or clarify.
7. In summary paragraph, please explain in a more clear manner what are the major finding and proved mechanism, instead of only simply re-stating the experimental observation.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
In the manuscript “Evidence of competing ground states between fractional Chern insulator and antiferromagnetism in moiré MoTe2”, Chang et. al. present a surprising result in the now famous twisted MoTe2 heterostructure device platform. Rather than fabricating devices in the ~3.7 degree range where the fractional quantum anomalous Hall effect was first discovered, the authors study dual gated devices with a twist angle of ~3 degrees. Unlike 3.7deg devices at hole doping of 1 hole per moiré unit cell, which present spontaneous symmetry breaking and an induced ferromagnetic state, they observe signatures of antiferromagnetic order, such as vanishing MCD signals and Hall resistivity at zero magnetic field. Further, the authors show that they can use electric fields to fully tune the AFM-FM transition in the device as well as an AFM to Chern insulating transition. I think the results are very exciting and open the door to another set of interesting phenomena in this rich system. The accessible interplay here between AFM, FM, and topological orders is an interesting one that warrants future work. However, I have reservations about recommending the manuscript for publication in its current form. The manuscript is lacking in many details and definitions that renders it unintelligible for any reader who is not already extremely knowledgeable about tMoTe2. Further exacerbating the problem, there is a heavy use of acronyms and shorthand that, again, might make the manuscript difficult to parse for a non-expert. I think that the data quality and analysis of the work is highly appropriate for Nature Communications and I think the results will be interesting and exciting to those working in condensed matter physics and 2D materials. As such, I recommend that the manuscript be accepted after major revisions of the written text to improve clarity. Please see my comments below.
-(Page 1, line 23) the authors have not defined what ν_h is. They should clarify that this is the hole filling factor for non-experts who read the manuscript.
-(Page 2, line 38) The manuscript never references Figure 1b
-(Page 3, line 1) The manuscript has not defined RC
-(Page 3, line 1) The authors are relatively unclear about whether they are tuning the hole doping of the system or the displacement field. I think simply mentioning ‘electric field’ is not enough given their dual-gated device geometry, they should be more specific.
-(Page 4, line 4) While the authors define Tw in the caption of ED fig. 9 and on page 7 they do not define it before its use here
-(Figure 1) the size and shape of the antiferromagnetic region in panel e is of a very similar size and shape as that of the ferromagnetic region in panel f and the bottom panel of figure 2a. Is there a connection here between the mechanisms that give rise to each magnetic ground state?
-(Figure 2) It would be very helpful for readers to label the filling factor on the panels of Figs. 2 b-e, in addition to where the authors have defined them in the caption, similarly to Fig. 3.
-(Page 4 line 7) The authors have left out the MCD subscript on chi
-(Page 4 line 10) In the hall resistivity data at v=1 filling, there still seems to be an appreciable plateau at 4K which seems to be missing from the MCD data. How do the authors explain this discrepancy?
-(Page 4 line 35) The claim here about the first pure electric field control of an AFM-FM transition may be true, but the result is similar in spirit to that of (Huang, B., Clark, G., Klein, D.R. et al. Electrical control of 2D magnetism in bilayer CrI3. Nature Nanotech 13, 544–548 (2018)). The authors should reference the article and provide the distinction between the works.
-(Figure 3) Panels d-e have no units on the field numbers of each panel. These plots should be readable without the caption and at present they are not.
-(Figure 4) again, no units on the E field values on panels b and d
-(Page 6 line 29) The authors repeatedly reference the critical field of switching the moire symmetry Ec but never state that value or indicate it on any of their plots. I think having a reference line on the plots or, at the very least, a statement of the field value of interest here would be helpful for readers so that they can understand the results without consulting the references.
-Throughout the paper, I found the use of abbreviations and lack of definitions/labels very hard to follow. I suggest the authors go through the manuscript carefully to ensure that all abbreviated names, commonly used letters and symbols, and figures are well defined/labeled.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
This manuscript investigates the correlated states of twisted MoTe2 (tMoTe2) for twist angles 2.4 – 4.1 using a combination of magnetic circular dichroism (MCD), reflection contrast (RC), exciton sensing and transport. The authors find an intermediate region of twist angle around 3 degrees where the valley-polarized ferromagnetic (VP-FM) integer and fractional Chern insulators at filling 1 and 2/3 filling are suppressed at small displacement fields E. Close to the displacement field Ec that layer polarizes the system, the VP-FM reemerges before transitioning to a layer polarized Mott insulator at E> Ec. The authors propose a charge-transfer mechanism to explain the emergence of this VP-FM close to Ec. The VP-FM state at filling 1 also reappears at smaller twist angles. Based on the M-H and \chi-T behavior, the authors propose that the ground state at intermediate angle and E is an out-of-plane antiferromagnet (VP-AFM).
While I believe this manuscript presents extensive novel experiments that will be of great interest to the community, I have some issues regarding the clarity of the arguments and calculations that I feel should be addressed before publication in Nature Communications.
1. Ref. [https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.22354] has performed nanoSQUID-on-tip on tMoTe2 for twist angles 2.1 to 3.7, finding VP-FM phases at filling 1 for all the angles, with a “triangular-like” shape of the VP-FM region similar to the one obtained in this study at angle 4.1 (which also contrasts with the 2.4 angle device of this work). What do the authors attribute these different phase diagrams to? Is there any clear difference in the samples, e.g.: what is the distance to the gates in each device? Can the authors estimate the disorder for the different twist angles?
2. Personally, I feel that, until reading the SI section 7, it is not clear that the authors propose that the AFM state has out-of-plane spins (it is VP-AFM), in contrast to the much more understood IVC-AFM with in-plane spins (see e.g. Refs. [10.1103/PhysRevX.13.041026], [10.1103/PhysRevB.109.L041106] for tMoTe2, and [arXiv:2503.09689], [10.1103/m6c2-yd5j] for tWSe2). I would suggest the authors to clarify this point better along the paper.
To the best of my knowledge, the VP-AFM is a new state which has not been observed in experiments or theoretical calculations of tTMDs. The signatures that the authors use to support the VP-AFM with respect to the IVC-AFM (and the IVC-FM) are based on two experimental measures: (1) The magnetization has a plateau at small H and then increases suddenly, and (2) The susceptibility peaks at a finite temperature. I agree with the authors that these signatures are not compatible with a collinear antiferromagnet with magnetic field applied perpendicular to the easy axis, but I’m wondering whether the same applies for an in-plane 120 antiferromagnet with strong Ising SOC (a positive magnetorresistance has also been observed for the IVC-AFM phase in tWSe2 [https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-08381-1]). I would appreciate if the authors could provide further comments or references for this.
3. The authors propose a charge transfer mechanism to explain the reemergent VP-FM close to the layer polarization transition at intermediate angles. However, at smaller and larger angles, the strongest VP-FM occurs at E=0, following the exchange mechanism. Is there any reason why intermediate angles are special?
4. Related to questions 2 and 3, in the discussion paragraph 18, I would suggest to clarify which type of AFM is predicted by the theory outside the VP-FM region; is it an IVC-AFM? If so, if the experimental ground state is really VP-AFM, this might have some implications for the exchange interactions / microscopic model assumed; would you expect these to change the charge transfer induced VP-FM? Are there any parameters in the phase diagram where the VP-AFM is the ground state?
5. Is it possible to determine whether the reemergent VP-FM state at the smallest twist angle is topological or trivial? Refs. [10.1103/PhysRevX.13.041026], [10.1103/PhysRevB.109.L041106] predicted a transition from the Chern insulator to a trivial VP-FM state at small twist angles at filling 1.
6. In page 4, lines 36-37, the authors state that “a pure electric-field-induced AFM-FM transition, which has never been observed in moiré systems and any other material systems, to the best of our knowledge”. A similar electric-field-induced trivial insulator to QAH transition has been observed in AB-MoTe2/WSe2 heterobilayers [https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-021-04171-1, 10.1103/PhysRevX.14.011004] (although it is true that it is not clear whether whether the trivial insulator is a Mott insulator or it has already ordered as an AFM at the experimental temperatures).
7. I was wondering whether it is possible to locate the (split) van Hove line in the density-displacement field diagram, and in this case whether its location coincides with the fillings 2/3 and/or 1 at the angles where the VP-FM disappears.
8. In SI 5 (see also Fig. 7e), the authors suggest that the non-monotonic behavior of Rxx as a function of T might be due to the AFM order decreasing Rxx by freezing the magnetic fluctuations, and then the gap opening or disorder increasing Rxx at lower T. I was wondering whether the measured Rxx could also be compatible with the scenario proposed in Ref. [10.1103/PhysRevX.12.021064], where Rxx decreases due to the appearance of an in-gap quasiparticle peak, which the magnetic ordering kills when it onsets at lower T.
9. 4. The meaning of RC (reflectance contract) should be defined before using it on page 3 line 1.
10. 5. While I understand that the authors refer to the layer polarization crossover/transition by “superlattice symmetry transition”, I think it might be a bit confusing, since the C2 symmetry that relates MX and XM is already broken by a finite displacement field. I would suggest changing this term by “layer polarization”, which is more commonly used in the literature, or explaining this terminology before using it (e.g. in the abstract).
11. In SI 1 page 2, I believe there is an errata: I think it should be t1 ~ sqrt(t2 U) instead of t2 ~ sqrt(t1 U). Also, in the Eq. At the top of page 2, I would suggest defining the interactions Ua, Ub beforehand. It would also be great if the authors could also explicitly say that \Delta ~ U.

The authors present a detailed study of tMoTe2 by tuning the twisting angle and vertical electric field, along with changing temperatures and magnetic fields, probed by both optical and electrical approaches. They focus on the magnetic states for samples of different conditions. The data sets are rich. There are a few major aspects the authors can improve before further consideration of this manuscript.
1. tMoTe2 is a system being intensively studied in the scientific field. What are the missing parts this work can contribute to? From both abstract and introduction, it is unclear what the new things this work brought to the community. The authors started with a brief introduction in abstract and introduction that tMoTe2 is a rich system in support of AQHE, but suddenly switched to talk about magnetism they found in this work. Some missing parts need to be provided so the readers can appreciate this work in the context of what has been and not been achieved in the field.

It is good to add brief legends to indicate the different conditions, based on which these data were acquired.
3. Mechanism. The authors suggest “charge transfer” as the mechanism. What are the charge transfer coming from? It is transferred from metal electrode to the tMoTe2, or self doping by transfer between the two layers of tMoTe2? Why is it not because of electric field effect? The authors have top and bottom electrodes, which allow them to separate electric field and electrostatic doping effects by tuning the top and bottom electrodes separately. ### Reviewer 3

This manuscript investigates the correlated states of twisted MoTe2 (tMoTe2) for twist angles 2.4 – 4.1 using a combination of magnetic circular dichroism (MCD), reflection contrast (RC), exciton sensing and transport. Close to the displacement field Ec that layer polarizes the system, the VP-FM reemerges before transitioning to a layer polarized Mott insulator at E> Ec. The authors propose a charge-transfer mechanism to explain the emergence of this VP-FM close to Ec. The VP-FM state at filling 1 also reappears at smaller twist angles. Based on the M-H and \chi-T behavior, the authors propose that the ground state at intermediate angle and E is an out-of-plane antiferromagnet (VP-AFM).

1. Ref. [https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.22354] has performed nanoSQUID-on-tip on tMoTe2 for twist angles 2.1 to 3.7, finding VP-FM phases at filling 1 for all the angles, with a “triangular-like” shape of the VP-FM region similar to the one obtained in this study at angle 4.1 (which also contrasts with the 2.4 angle device of this work). Personally, I feel that, until reading the SI section 7, it is not clear that the authors propose that the AFM state has out-of-plane spins (it is VP-AFM), in contrast to the much more understood IVC-AFM with in-plane spins (see e.g. Refs. electric‑field control of magnetism and topology.

## Introduction

The interplay between strong correlations and topology can lead to the emergence of intriguing
quantum states of matter. Moiré materials based on transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) have
emerged as a promising platform for exploring novel quantum phenomena that arise from band
topology and many-body interactions1–12. Recently, there has been a surge in research focused on
rhombohedral-stacked (R-stacked) tMoTe , in which transport experiments have provided
2
unambiguous evidence of both QAH and FQAH effects on devices with relatively large twist
angles 𝜃 ∼ 3.7°−3.9° 13,14. Based on the obtained Chern numbers, photoluminescence and
compressibility measurements suggest the FQAH is the ground state of 𝑣 = 2/3 (𝜈 = 1 is
h h
defined as one hole per moiré unit cell, corresponding to a half-filled moiré valence band) over a
relatively large range of twist angle, specifically 𝜃~2.6°−3.9°, while QAH at 𝑣 = 1 extends
h
even down to 2.1°14–19. The Chern numbers were obtained by comparing the Streda formula with
the fitted dispersion slope of the filling factor versus the magnetic field (𝐵 ) of Tesla order.
However, the energy difference between the competing phases is usually subtle, and the applied
relatively large 𝐵 could hide the true ground state at zero 𝐵. Transport measurement can provide
unambiguous evidence of the true ground state as demonstrated in devices with relatively large
twist angles (𝜃 ∼ 3.7°−3.9°), while transport study of 𝑣 ≤ 1 states in tMoTe moiré device with
h 2
small 𝜃 is challenging due to the increasing difficulty of making transparent electrical contact. On
the other hand, in the moiré system, the ground states are usually expected to be sensitive to the
twist angle22, suggesting more unexpected correlated effects to explore in tMoTe moiré system
2
with smaller 𝜃19–24.

In this work, we performed a systematic twist angle dependence study on the R-stacked tMoTe
2
moiré system by combining optical and transport measurements. We observed competing magnetic
ground states depending on both twist angle and 𝐸. Specifically, we observed unexpected AFM
ground states with vanishing Hall resistance at both 𝑣 = 1 and 2/3, at intermediate twist angles
h
𝜃~3° , in between the FMCCI ground states of both larger and smaller 𝜃 . Moreover, applying
vertical electric field (𝐸) induces an AFM to FM (ICICFCI) transition and an emergent FM state
was observed near critical electric field (𝐸 ) of layer polarization.

### Reviewer 3

This manuscript investigates the correlated states of twisted MoTe2 (tMoTe2) for twist angles 2.4 – 4.1 using a combination of magnetic circular dichroism (MCD), reflection contrast (RC), exciton sensing and transport. The authors find an intermediate region of twist angle around 3 degrees where the valley-polarized ferromagnetic (VP-FM) integer and fractional Chern insulators at filling 1 and 2/3 filling are suppressed at small displacement fields E. Close to the displacement field Ec that layer polarizes the system, the VP-FM reemerges before transitioning to a layer polarized Mott insulator at E> Ec. The authors propose a charge-transfer mechanism to explain the emergence of this VP-FM close to Ec. The VP-FM state at filling 1 also reappears at smaller twist angles. Based on the M-H and \chi-T behavior, the authors propose that the ground state at intermediate angle and E is an out-of-plane antiferromagnet (VP-AFM).
While I believe this manuscript presents extensive novel experiments that will be of great interest to the community, I have some issues regarding the clarity of the arguments and calculations that I feel should be addressed before publication in Nature Communications.
1. Ref. [https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.22354] has performed nanoSQUID-on-tip on tMoTe2 for twist angles 2.1 to 3.7, finding VP-FM phases at filling 1 for all the angles, with a “triangular-like” shape of the VP-FM region similar to the one obtained in this study at angle 4.1 (which also contrasts with the 2.4 angle device of this work). What do the authors attribute these different phase diagrams to? Is there any clear difference in the samples, e.g.: what is the distance to the gates in each device? Can the authors estimate the disorder for the different twist angles?
2. Personally, I feel that, until reading the SI section 7, it is not clear that the authors propose that the AFM state has out-of-plane spins (it is VP-AFM), in contrast to the much more understood IVC-AFM with in-plane spins (see e.g. Refs. [10.1103/PhysRevX.13.041026], [10.1103/PhysRevB.109.L041106] for tMoTe2, and [arXiv:2503.09689], [10.1103/m6c2-yd5j] for tWSe2). I would suggest the authors to clarify this point better along the paper.
To the best of my knowledge, the VP-AFM is a new state which has not been observed in experiments or theoretical calculations of tTMDs. The signatures that the authors use to support the VP-AFM with respect to the IVC-AFM (and the IVC-FM) are based on two experimental measures: (1) The magnetization has a plateau at small H and then increases suddenly, and (2) The susceptibility peaks at a finite temperature. I agree with the authors that these signatures are not compatible with a collinear antiferromagnet with magnetic field applied perpendicular to the easy axis, but I’m wondering whether the same applies for an in-plane 120 antiferromagnet with strong Ising SOC (a positive magnetorresistance has also been observed for the IVC-AFM phase in tWSe2 [https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-08381-1]). 5. Is it possible to determine whether the reemergent VP-FM state at the smallest twist angle is topological or trivial? Refs. [10.1103/PhysRevX.13.041026], [10.1103/PhysRevB.109.L041106] predicted a transition from the Chern insulator to a trivial VP-FM state at small twist angles at filling 1.

In the manuscript “Evidence of competing ground states between fractional Chern
insulator and antiferromagnetism in moiré MoTe2”, Chang et. al. present a surprising
result in the now famous twisted MoTe2 heterostructure device platform. Rather than
fabricating devices in the ~3.7 degree range where the fractional quantum anomalous
Hall effect was first discovered, the authors study dual gated devices with a twist angle
of ~3 degrees. Unlike 3.7deg devices at hole doping of 1 hole per moiré unit cell, which
present spontaneous symmetry breaking and an induced ferromagnetic state, they
observe signatures of antiferromagnetic order, such as vanishing MCD signals and Hall
resistivity at zero magnetic field. Further, the authors show that they can use electric
fields to fully tune the AFM-FM transition in the device as well as an AFM to Chern
insulating transition. I think the results are very exciting and open the door to another
set of interesting phenomena in this rich system. The accessible interplay here between
AFM, FM, and topological orders is an interesting one that warrants future work.
However, I have reservations about recommending the manuscript for publication in its
 its
current form. The manuscript is lacking in many details and definitions that renders it
unintelligible for any reader who is not already extremely knowledgeable about tMoTe2.
Further exacerbating the problem, there is a heavy use of acronyms and shorthand that,
again, might make the manuscript difficult to parse for a non-expert. I think that the
data quality and analysis of the work is highly appropriate for Nature Communications
and I think the results will be interesting and exciting to those working in condensed
matter physics and 2D materials. As such, I recommend that the manuscript be accepted
after major revisions of the written text to improve clarity. Please see my comments
below.

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
Overall comment:
This manuscript investigates the correlated states of twisted MoTe2 (tMoTe2) for twist
angles 2.4 – 4.1 using a combination of magnetic circular dichroism (MCD), reflection
contrast (RC), exciton sensing and transport. The authors find an intermediate region
of twist angle around 3 degrees where the valley-polarized ferromagnetic (VP-FM)
integer and fractional Chern insulators at filling 1 and 2/3 filling are suppressed at small
displacement fields E. Close to the displacement field Ec that layer polarizes the system,
the VP-FM reemerges before transitioning to a layer polarized Mott insulator at E> Ec.
The authors propose a charge-transfer mechanism to explain the emergence of this VP-
FM close to Ec. The VP-FM state at filling 1 also reappears at smaller twist angles.
Based on the M-H and \chi-T behavior, the authors propose that the ground state at
intermediate angle and E is an out-of-plane antiferromagnet (VP-AFM).
While I believe this manuscript presents extensive novel experiments that will be of
great interest to the community, I have some issues regarding the clarity of the
arguments and calculations that I feel should be addressed before publication in Nature
Communications.

1) As pointed out by the reviewer, it could be related to the different thickness of the
dielectric layer. Typically, we use relatively thin hBN <10 nm for better optical contrast
and larger (n, E) tuning range [Nature 600, 641]. Specifically, for the main device
studied here, we used hBN ~8 nm. This is close to the moire lattice constant of ~ 7 nm,
where the dielectric screening could start to play a role. It has been demonstrated that

2) It could be related to the difference in the twisted angle and the angle calibration

Comment #23: The authors propose a charge transfer mechanism to explain the
reemergent VP-FM close to the layer polarization transition at intermediate angles.
However, at smaller and larger angles, the strongest VP-FM occurs at E=0, following
the exchange mechanism. Is there any reason why intermediate angles are special?
Response #23: We thank the reviewer for this thoughtful question. In tMoTe , the
2
magnetic order is governed by the competition between kinetic exchange and intersite
Hund’s coupling (the latter favoring ferromagnetism). At both very small and very large
twist angles, Hund’s coupling dominates and the ground state is ferromagnetic. At
intermediate angles (≈3°), the kinetic-exchange contribution prevails, likely due to a
topological transition between the second and third bands, changing their Chern
numbers from (1,1) at large angles to (1,−1) near 3° [Communications Physics 7, 262
(2024)].

2,

insufficient to determine the spin configuration of the AFM state unambiguously.

I thank the authors for their detailed responses and appropriate changes to the manuscript. I recommend publication in Nature Communications once these minor comments are addressed.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

The authors present a detailed study of tMoTe2 by tuning the twisting angle and vertical electric field, along with changing temperatures and magnetic fields, probed by both optical and electrical approaches. They focus on the magnetic states for samples of different conditions. The data sets are rich. There are a few major aspects the authors can improve before further consideration of this manuscript.
1. tMoTe2 is a system being intensively studied in the scientific field. What are the missing parts this work can contribute to? From both abstract and introduction, it is unclear what the new things this work brought to the community. The authors started with a brief introduction in abstract and introduction that tMoTe2 is a rich system in support of AQHE, but suddenly switched to talk about magnetism they found in this work. Some missing parts need to be provided so the readers can appreciate this work in the context of what has been and not been achieved in the field.
2. The readability of most figures is still low. It seems that figure 1d-f and 1g-I have one-to-one corresponding relationship. However, from these sub-figures themselves, it is hard to read since g and h have the same legend yet different curves. The same issue is for Figure b and c (these two sub-figures have the same noted curves), d and e. It is good to add brief legends to indicate the different conditions, based on which these data were acquired.
3. Mechanism. The authors suggest “charge transfer” as the mechanism. What are the charge transfer coming from? It is transferred from metal electrode to the tMoTe2, or self doping by transfer between the two layers of tMoTe2? Why is it not because of electric field effect? The authors have top and bottom electrodes, which allow them to separate electric field and electrostatic doping effects by tuning the top and bottom electrodes separately. If the magnetic anisotropy is in-plane, it is likely the out of plane B field would gradually increase the MCD, and it is also likely that out of plane B field would cause spin flop effect suddenly at a certain B field.

### Reviewer 3

This manuscript investigates the correlated states of twisted MoTe2 (tMoTe2) for twist angles 2.4 – 4.1 using a combination of magnetic circular dichroism (MCD), reflection contrast (RC), exciton sensing and transport. The authors find an intermediate region of twist angle around 3 degrees where the valley-polarized ferromagnetic (VP-FM) integer and fractional Chern insulators at filling 1 and 2/3 filling are suppressed at small displacement fields E. Close to the displacement field Ec that layer polarizes the system, the VP-FM reemerges before transitioning to a layer polarized Mott insulator at E> Ec. The authors propose a charge-transfer mechanism to explain the emergence of this VP-FM close to Ec. The VP-FM state at filling 1 also reappears at smaller twist angles. Based on the M-H and \chi-T behavior, the authors propose that the ground state at intermediate angle and E is an out-of-plane antiferromagnet (VP-AFM).
While I believe this manuscript presents extensive novel experiments that will be of great interest to the community, I have some issues regarding the clarity of the arguments and calculations that I feel should be addressed before publication in Nature Communications.
1. Ref. [https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.22354] has performed nanoSQUID-on-tip on tMoTe2 for twist angles 2.1 to 3.7, finding VP-FM phases at filling 1 for all the angles, with a “triangular-like” shape of the VP-FM region similar to the one obtained in this study at angle 4.1 (which also contrasts with the 2.4 angle device of this work). What do the authors attribute these different phase diagrams to? Is there any clear difference in the samples, e.g.: what is the distance to the gates in each device? Can the authors estimate the disorder for the different twist angles?
2. Personally, I feel that, until reading the SI section 7, it is not clear that the authors propose that the AFM state has out-of-plane spins (it is VP-AFM), in contrast to the much more understood IVC-AFM with in-plane spins (see e.g. Refs. [10.1103/PhysRevX.13.041026], [10.1103/PhysRevB.109.L041106] for tMoTe2, and [arXiv:2503.09689], [10.1103/m6c2-yd5j] for tWSe2). I would suggest the authors to clarify this point better along the paper.
To the best of my knowledge, the VP-AFM is a new state which has not been observed in experiments or theoretical calculations of tTMDs. The signatures that the authors use to support the VP-AFM with respect to the IVC-AFM (and the IVC-FM) are based on two experimental measures: (1) The magnetization has a plateau at small H and then increases suddenly, and (2) The susceptibility peaks at a finite temperature. I agree with the authors that these signatures are not compatible with a collinear antiferromagnet with magnetic field applied perpendicular to the easy axis, but I’m wondering whether the same applies for an in-plane 120 antiferromagnet with strong Ising SOC (a positive magnetorresistance has also been observed for the IVC-AFM phase in tWSe2 [https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-08381-1]). I would appreciate if the authors could provide further comments or references for this.
3. The authors propose a charge transfer mechanism to explain the reemergent VP-FM close to the layer polarization transition at intermediate angles. However, at smaller and larger angles, the strongest VP-FM occurs at E=0, following the exchange mechanism. Is there any reason why intermediate angles are special?
4. Related to questions 2 and 3, in the discussion paragraph 18, I would suggest to clarify which type of AFM is predicted by the theory outside the VP-FM region; is it an IVC-AFM? If so, if the experimental ground state is really VP-AFM, this might have some implications for the exchange interactions / microscopic model assumed; would you expect these to change the charge transfer induced VP-FM? Are there any parameters in the phase diagram where the VP-AFM is the ground state?
5. Is it possible to determine whether the reemergent VP-FM state at the smallest twist angle is topological or trivial? Refs. [10.1103/PhysRevX.13.041026], [10.1103/PhysRevB.109.L041106] predicted a transition from the Chern insulator to a trivial VP-FM state at small twist angles at filling 1.
6. In page 4, lines 36-37, the authors state that “a pure electric-field-induced AFM-FM transition, which has never been observed in moiré systems and any other material systems, to the best of our knowledge”.
